n101.text: Last time, Basil changed two things at once, so his test was not fair. In a fair test, we change only one thing.

n201m.text: Here is my plan! Set-up X and set-up Y.

n202.text: A little sparrow is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

n204.text: Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

n401.text: Round one. Momo wants to find out if more batteries make an electromagnet stronger. Set-up X has one battery and ten turns. Set-up Y has two batteries and twenty turns. Is her test fair? One, yes. Two, no, two things changed. Three, no, use a steel nail. Show me your fingers.

n403m.text: One! X and Y are both electromagnets, so it is a fair race.

n404p.text: Three. Basil's steel nail is still here. We should use it.

n405b.text: Two! Momo changed the batteries and the turns. I did that too, last time!

n501.text: The answer is two! Did you show two fingers? Put one finger up!

n503b.text: A prediction is what we think will happen, such as: more batteries will make our electromagnet stronger!

n601p.text: There are so many things on the bench. How do we keep track of them all?

n602.text: Look closer. Here is our plan. The variable to be changed is the number of batteries.

n603.text: The variables to be kept the same are the type of batteries, the type of steel clips, the type of iron nail, and the number of turns of wire around the iron nail.

n604.text: The variable to be measured is the number of steel clips attracted.

n605m.text: The variable to be measured is the one thing we count or measure, such as the number of steel clips attracted!

n607.text: When we increase the number of batteries, the strength of the electromagnet will increase.

n701.text: Showdown! Double points. Pip's plan card has one mistake. Line one, two, or three? Show me with your fingers.

n702p.text: One: change only the number of batteries. Two: keep everything else the same. Three: count the clips once, and we are done!

n704b.text: Three! One count is not enough. Scientists repeat the test a few times.

n705.text: Three fingers? Put up two more on your score hand!

n801.text: Be a steel paper clip! Shrink down. Quietly.

n802.text: You are a steel paper clip in the tray. The nail with two batteries comes down. You jump up, and cling to its tip!

n803.text: A giant hand counts you and the other clips. Then back you go into the tray, and up again. Count after count.

n804.text: Nine clips. Then eight. Then nine again.

n901m.text: But Pip counted only once, and got seven. Which count is right?

n902.text: Look closer. One count can trick us. A clip may slip off, or we may count too fast.

n903.text: When we count again and again, the counts are close to each other. Nine, eight, nine. And with one battery: five, six, five. Our prediction was right!

n904p.text: Reliable means we can trust the results, because we get nearly the same results each time we repeat the test, such as nine, eight and nine clips!

n907.text: It is also important to repeat the experiment a few times to ensure that the results are reliable.

c1003.text: Change? Only one thing! The others? Kept the same! Test it once? No! Repeat it!

n1101.text: Show me your score hand! Two fingers or more? You beat the Buddies. Three fingers? High five!

n1102.text: Did you spot the sparrow? It was on the railing, just outside the door!

n1103p.text: Here is a fun fact! A sparrow's heart beats hundreds of times in one minute! Scientists count it again and again, to be sure.

n1201.text: Next time: Pip pushes his fridge door gently. It swings shut by itself, and stays closed. There is no lock and no catch. What keeps it closed? One, the cold air inside. Two, a strip of magnet. Three, sticky glue. Lock in your answer!
